seoTitle: How to Overlay Images in Canva Easily
metaDescription: Stack and layer multiple images in Canva using the layers panel, transparency adjustments, and background removal for clean composites.
intro: Creating a professional composite from multiple images means managing layer order, transparency, and backgrounds carefully. Canva's layers panel gives you the tools to stack images without disrupting your overall canvas layout. This guide covers positioning, transparency, and grouping so your overlays stay exactly where you want them.

steps.heading: Open the layers panel
steps.body: Locate the Position menu and Layers panel tab to begin managing your image stack.

steps.heading: Place your initial images
steps.body: Upload and position the images you want to overlay on the canvas.

steps.heading: Adjust layer hierarchy
steps.body: Reorder the stack so images appear in the correct front-to-back sequence.

steps.heading: Remove backgrounds where needed
steps.body: Use the built-in background remover tool on foreground elements for seamless stacking.

steps.heading: Modify transparency and blending
steps.body: Adjust the opacity of overlay images to achieve the visual effect you're after.

steps.heading: Export the finished composite
steps.body: Group elements to lock their positions, then export the multi-layered design as a high-resolution PNG.

faq.question: How do I stop an image from covering another one unintentionally?
faq.answer: Adjusting the layer hierarchy in the Layers panel lets you control which image sits in front of or behind another.

faq.question: Can I make an overlay image semi-transparent?
faq.answer: Yes, transparency and opacity settings can be adjusted for any image layer to create blending effects.

faq.question: Do I need to remove the background before overlaying an image?
faq.answer: It's usually necessary for a clean composite, since a solid background would otherwise block the layers beneath it.

faq.question: Will grouping my layered images prevent accidental changes?
faq.answer: Yes, grouping elements together helps lock their relative position so they move as one unit and are less likely to shift accidentally.
